paras: The attempted lynching of Vine Bryant took place on May 15, 1903, in the Fulton circuit court at Hickman, Kentucky, when spectators rushed a Black defendant on trial for shooting a young white man. Sheriff Carpenter held the crowd back while deputies took Bryant out of the courthouse and on to the Eddyville penitentiary, where he was to serve a five-year sentence. Kentucky papers reported it as a lynching averted only by the officers' quick action, and the story was reprinted as far away as Wichita.

On a Sunday afternoon in September 1902, Leslie Hackett, a white youth of 18, was shot in the back at Hickman by Vine Bryant, described by a Union City, Tennessee, paper as 'a colored restaurant keeper, and alleged illicit whiskey vender.' According to that report, the two had quarreled earlier in the day and had been jailed by City Marshal Dillon and then released, after which Bryant got his pistol and shot Hackett 'without warning.' The same paper said there was talk of 'mob treatment for the negro' that night, which was avoided, and added that Hackett had 'kept bad company' and dealt in 'bootleg' whiskey.

A week later a Hickman dispatch to the Paducah Sun said Hackett was still alive, that Bryant's trial was set for October and that 'excitement is about over.' The Hickman Courier reported that Hackett was taken to Cairo on the "Rees Lee" for an X-ray to locate the bullet, and that his mother followed in the company of Sheriff Carpenter.

The case came to trial in May 1903. According to a special dispatch to the Louisville Courier-Journal, Bryant testified in his own behalf that he struck Hackett on the head with a pistol and shot him in the back as Hackett turned to get away. At this, the spectators 'rose as one man' and, shouting 'hang him,' surged forward to seize the prisoner.

Sheriff Carpenter stepped between the crowd and the defendant and held it back while deputies took Bryant out a back door, put him in a wagon and drove out of town. They took him to a point on the Nashville, Chattanooga and St. Louis railroad, where they boarded a train for Eddyville, the site of the state penitentiary.

The jury found Bryant guilty without leaving their seats, and he was sentenced to five years in the Eddyville penitentiary. Hackett was reported still confined to his bed with a paralytic stroke caused by the bullet's injury to his spine. No report of arrests or of any action against the crowd was found.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, and most of it from Kentucky. The Courier-Journal printed its Fulton special on May 16 under the headline 'Furious Rush Made For Negro Prisoner At Hickman,' with the subheads 'Officers Hurried Him Away to State Prison to Save Him From Lynching' and 'Shot a Young White Man.' The same day the paper summarized the case on its front page, and the Paducah Sun carried a short Hickman dispatch headed 'Negro Given Five Years at Hickman.'

The Courier-Journal's account described Hackett as 'a young white man of high standing' and credited the sheriff's 'prompt action' with preventing the lynching, without comment on the crowd itself. The Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal reprinted the front-page brief on May 19. On May 22 the Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Fulton special nearly word for word under the headline 'Mob Spirit Rife,' with a May 21 dateline. No coverage in the Black press was found.

Because the Wichita reprint carried a May 21 dateline, the event has also been dated to that day, but the Louisville and Paducah papers printed the story on May 16 and place the trial on May 15. Accounts of the shooting also differ: the 1902 report has Bryant firing from behind without warning, while the 1903 dispatch has him admitting a blow with the pistol before he fired as Hackett turned away.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Vine Bryant
bases: Courtroom spectators shouting 'hang him' surged forward to seize a Black defendant and were held off by the sheriff while deputies removed him, an attempted lynching of a prisoner in custody (A5, A6, A8).

Bryant was not killed: deputies removed him from the courtroom and took him to the Eddyville penitentiary (A5, A6); the crowd's rush to seize and 'hang' him for shooting a white man makes this an attempted lynching, not a completed one (A5, A8).

The Courier-Journal's Fulton special and a separate Hickman dispatch in the Paducah Sun agree that officers rushed Bryant from the courtroom to save him from lynching after a five-year sentence (A5, A6), and the 1902 background is confirmed by three papers (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Courier-Journal special from Fulton
accounts.gist: Bryant admitted on the stand that he struck Hackett with a pistol and shot him in the back; spectators rose shouting 'hang him' and only the sheriff's prompt action prevented a lynching.

accounts.label: Hickman dispatch to the Paducah Sun
accounts.gist: Bryant was given five years and officers had to rush him from the court room to save him from lynching.

accounts.label: Union City report of the 1902 shooting
accounts.gist: After a morning quarrel and arrest, Bryant got his pistol and shot Hackett in the back without warning; the paper added that Hackett kept bad company and was involved in 'bootleg' whiskey dealings.

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal headlined a 'Furious Rush Made For Negro Prisoner' and praised the 'prompt action of Sheriff Carpenter', while stressing that Hackett was 'a young white man of high standing'.
The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Fulton special as 'Mob Spirit Rife' with the subhead 'Trial in Kentucky Court Comes Near Ending in Lynching'.
The Paducah Sun and the Courier-Journal's front page treated it as a short news item about the sentence, noting the removal 'to save him from lynching'.
The Union City Commercial in 1902 called the shooting unprovoked ('without warning') but said young Hackett 'has kept bad company' and came to grief through 'bootleg' whiskey.

versions.value: May 15, 1903 (dateline May 15 'today'; Hickman dispatch of May 16 says 'yesterday')

conflicts.note: The story was in print in Louisville and Paducah on May 16, so the Wichita dateline of May 21 cannot be the event date; May 15 is supported by two earlier Kentucky papers.

versions.value: Bryant struck Hackett on the head with a pistol and shot him in the back as Hackett turned to get away (Bryant's own testimony as reported)
Bryant got his pistol, walked up behind a party including Hackett and shot him in the back without warning

conflicts.note: Both versions have Hackett shot in the back; they differ on whether a blow with the pistol came first. The 1902 account is the nearer in time; the 1903 one is presented as Bryant's own admission.

threat only: a courtroom crowd rushed the prisoner shouting 'hang him'; no siege of a jail was reported
Leslie Hackett was wounded in the September 1902 shooting that led to the trial, not in this episode
The 1903 coverage begins 1903-05-16; the underlying shooting was covered from 1902-09-26
